chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn al-Hamid al-Attar, from Yunus ibn Yaqub, from Umar the brother of Udhafir, who said:

A man handed over to me six hundred or seven hundred dirhams for Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him). So it was in my bag. When I arrived at Al-Hafeera, my bag split and everything in it was taken. I met the governor of the city there, and he said, 'Are you the one whose bag split and belongings were taken?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'When we arrive in the city, come to me so that I may compensate you.'

He said: So when I arrived in the city, I entered upon Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him). He said, 'O Umar, your bag split and your belongings were taken?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'What Allah gave you is better than what was taken from you. The Messenger of Allah's (peace be upon him and his family) she-camel got lost, so the people said regarding it, 'He informs us about the sky but does not inform us about his she-camel.' Then Gabriel (peace be upon him) descended and said, 'O Muhammad, your she-camel is in such and such a valley, its bridle entangled with such and such a tree.'

He said: So he ascended the pulpit, praised Allah and extolled Him, and said, 'O people, you have burdened me regarding my she-camel. Indeed, what Allah gave me is better than what was taken from me. Indeed, my she-camel is in such and such a valley, its bridle entangled with such and such a tree.' So the people rushed towards it and found her as the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) had said. He then said, 'Go to the governor of the city and take from him what he promised you, for it is something Allah invited you to; you did not seek it from him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the story of the lost dirhams and the Prophet's she-camel in al-Kafi?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Umar ibn Udhafir narrates the loss of dirhams entrusted to Imam al-Sadiq (AS), who comforts him by comparing the incident to the Prophet’s lost she-camel, emphasizing that divine revelation and knowledge outweigh material possessions. The Imam advises Umar to seek compensation from the governor, framing the event as a divine invitation rather than a mere loss, thereby illustrating the Shia concept of *fadilat al-'ilm* (superiority of knowledge) over worldly wealth. This narrative reinforces the Imam’s role as the interpreter of divine will, where even mundane losses carry spiritual significance and are resolved through his guidance.
